why: Every company plans its year, then explains every month why reality differs from the plan. FP&A analysts and management controllers build the budget and the forecasts, explain the variances and help managers decide: it is one of the most common entry points into corporate finance, and the interviews test both the numbers and how you explain them.
outcome: run an annual budget cycle, build driver-based and rolling forecasts, explain budget vs actual with price, volume and mix variances that add up, separate fixed and variable costs, allocate overheads, compute a break-even, produce a month-end reporting pack with a bridge and challenge a budget as a business partner.

lessons.title: What FP&A and management control do
text: FP&A (financial planning and analysis) looks forward: it builds the budget, updates the forecast during the year and analyses what drives the results. Management control, called contrôle de gestion in France, covers the same ground with more weight on cost control, cost accounting and monthly reporting. In many French companies the contrôleur de gestion does both jobs; in US and UK groups the FP&A team is usually separate from the controllership team that owns the books.

The difference with accounting matters in interviews. Accounting records what happened, following IFRS or local GAAP (US GAAP in the United States, the French PCG for statutory accounts), and closes the books. FP&A takes those closed numbers and answers three questions: where are we against the plan, why, and where will we land at year end? Management reporting does not have to follow IFRS: it can use EBITDA, contribution margin or constant-currency growth, as long as the definitions are stable and reconcile to the published accounts.

A typical week mixes routine and analysis. The routine: the month-end pack, the forecast update, the headcount report. The analysis: why did gross margin fall two points in the south region, is this investment case credible, what happens to cash if a large client pays 30 days later? The value of an analyst is in the second part, and the first part must be automated enough to leave time for it.

FP&A sits between finance and the business. Each analyst is often the finance partner of a business unit or a department: they know its drivers (volumes, prices, headcount, conversion rates), meet its managers every month and turn their plans into numbers. That is why job offers ask for Excel and a reporting tool, but also for communication and the ability to challenge a manager politely.
points: FP&A looks forward (budget, forecast, analysis); accounting records and closes the past.
Contrôle de gestion = management control: cost control, cost accounting, reporting, often FP&A as well.
Management reporting can use non-IFRS measures (EBITDA, contribution margin) if they reconcile to the published accounts.
Three questions every month: where are we, why, where will we land?
Automate the routine so the time goes to analysis.

example.code:
FP&A team (finance department, reports to the CFO)
├─ Budget and forecasts      plan the year, update the outlook
├─ Monthly reporting         actual vs budget, KPIs, commentary
├─ Business partnering       one analyst per business unit
└─ Ad hoc analysis           pricing, investment cases, scenarios

Accounting closes the books  →  FP&A explains the numbers  →  managers decide
example.note: The same work is called FP&A in a US-style group and contrôle de gestion in many French companies.

lessons.title: The annual budget cycle
text: The budget is the financial plan for next year, month by month: revenue, costs, headcount, capital expenditure (capex) and, in better processes, cash. It sets the targets managers are measured against and the spending they are allowed. Most companies on a calendar year start in September and finish when the board approves the budget in December.

There are two directions. Top-down: management sets the targets (for example +8 % revenue, EBITDA margin of 15 %) and the departments must fit inside them. Bottom-up: each department builds its numbers from its own drivers, finance adds them up. Top-down is fast but ignores what the teams know; bottom-up is realistic but slow and usually too optimistic on revenue and too generous on costs. Most companies combine them: top-down guidelines first, bottom-up build, then iterations until the two meet.

Finance sends guidelines before the build so everyone uses the same assumptions: inflation and salary increases, FX rates, headcount rules, the template and the timetable. Without them, every department uses its own exchange rate and the consolidation becomes a negotiation about assumptions instead of a discussion about the business.

Zero-based budgeting (ZBB, budget base zéro) starts every cost line from zero: each expense must be justified by what it delivers, instead of last year plus 3 %. It finds savings in overheads such as travel, consultants or software licences, but it takes much more time, so companies use it every few years or on selected cost areas. Incremental budgeting (last year plus or minus a percentage) is the common default and quietly keeps every old expense.

In real jobs the budget is late, the first version misses the target, and the third iteration is about where to cut. Keep a version log (v1 submitted, v2 after review, v3 approved), lock the approved version in the reporting tool and never overwrite it: you will compare against it all year.
points: Top-down sets targets, bottom-up builds from drivers; most companies iterate between the two.
Guidelines first: inflation, salary increases, FX rates, headcount rules, template, timetable.
Zero-based budgeting justifies each cost from zero; incremental budgeting is last year plus or minus a percentage.
Lock the approved budget and keep a version log: it is the reference for the whole year.

example.code:
Budget timetable for calendar year N (example)
Sep N-1   Finance sends guidelines: growth target, inflation, FX rates, headcount rules
Sep-Oct   Departments build their budgets from drivers (volumes, prices, headcount)
Oct       Finance consolidates, checks against targets, challenges the gaps
Nov       Executive review, second round of changes
Dec       Board approves the budget
Jan N     Budget loaded into the reporting tool; monthly tracking starts
example.note: Calendar-year company; with a fiscal year starting in April, the whole timetable moves.

lessons.title: Forecasting: driver-based, rolling forecasts, run-rate, seasonality
text: The budget is fixed once approved; the forecast is updated during the year to show where the year will land (the outlook, atterrissage in French). Many companies re-forecast quarterly: a 3+9 forecast uses 3 months of actuals and 9 months of forecast, then 6+6 and 9+3. A rolling forecast always looks the same distance ahead, for example 12 or 18 months, whatever the calendar, so the horizon never shrinks to a few weeks in November.

A driver-based forecast models the numbers from their operational causes instead of extending totals. Revenue = active customers × average revenue per user (ARPU); customers at the end of the month = opening customers × (1 − churn rate) + new customers; payroll = headcount × average cost. When sales says new customers will drop, you change one driver and every line follows. The art is in choosing few drivers that really explain the numbers and that someone in the business owns.

A run-rate extends the recent pace: year-to-date actuals plus the average of the last months times the months left. With January to June at 410, 425, 398, 440, 452 and 461 (thousand euros), the year to date is 2,586 and the last three months average 451, so the full-year run-rate is 2,586 + 451 × 6 = 5,292. It is a quick sanity check, not a forecast: it ignores seasonality, signed contracts and price increases.

Seasonality is the regular pattern inside a year: retail peaks in December, travel in summer, B2B software sales in the last month of each quarter. A seasonal index (each month's share of the annual total, from several past years) spreads an annual number over the months: if December is usually 12 % of the year and the target is 1.2 million, December is planned at 144,000. Comparing a month with the same month last year, rather than with the previous month, also removes most of the seasonality.

Track forecast accuracy: compare each forecast with the actual it predicted, as a percentage error, and look for a bias. A forecast that is always 5 % too high is not unlucky; it has an optimistic driver, and management will learn to discount it.
points: Budget fixed, forecast updated: 3+9, 6+6, 9+3, or a rolling forecast that always looks 12-18 months ahead.
Driver-based: revenue = customers × ARPU, payroll = headcount × average cost.
Run-rate = year to date + recent monthly average × months left; a sanity check, not a forecast.
Seasonal index = a month's share of the year; compare with the same month last year.
Measure forecast accuracy and bias every month.

example.note: B9 run-rate; C14 customers = opening × (1 − churn in B1) + new customers in B2; D14 revenue = customers × ARPU in B3; E14 annual target in B20 × the seasonal index of the month in row 1.

lessons.title: Budget vs actual: favourable, unfavourable, materiality, commentary
text: Variance = actual − budget, and variance % = variance / budget. The sign alone does not say whether it is good news: more revenue than budget is favourable (F), more cost than budget is unfavourable (U). To avoid confusion, many teams show costs as positive numbers and compute the variance so that a positive number is always favourable (budget − actual for costs), or add an F/U column. Pick one convention and write it on the report.

Compare like with like. If the budget was built at an exchange rate of 1.10 dollars per euro and the actual rate was 1.05, part of the variance is currency, not performance: show it separately or restate at budget rates (constant currency). The same applies to a business bought during the year (scope effect) or to a calendar effect (one more working day). Flexed budgets go further: they restate the cost budget at the actual volume, so a production manager is not blamed for costs that rose only because sales were higher.

Not every variance deserves a comment. Teams set materiality thresholds, for example a variance above 5 % and above 10,000 euros, or the top five variances by amount. Below the threshold, no comment; above it, an explanation is required. Without a threshold, the pack fills up with comments on 300-euro differences and the real story disappears.

A good commentary explains the cause, the amount and what happens next. "Revenue +20k, higher than budget" repeats the table. "Revenue +20k (+4 %): 2 new retail clients signed in March (+26k), partly offset by lower prices on the Nordics contract (−6k); both effects continue, the full-year forecast is raised by 60k" tells the reader something. Say whether the variance is a timing difference (spending moved to next month) or permanent (the money is gone or earned).
points: Variance = actual − budget; variance % = variance / budget; state F or U.
More revenue or less cost = favourable; less revenue or more cost = unfavourable.
Separate FX (constant currency), scope and calendar effects from performance; flex the budget for volume.
Materiality threshold: comment only what is above, for example 5 % and 10k.
Commentary = cause + amount + timing or permanent + impact on the forecast.

example.note: Costs are positive numbers; a cost variance is shown as budget − actual so that + is always favourable.

lessons.title: Price, volume and mix variances
text: When revenue or margin differs from the budget, the first question in any review is: did we sell more, at a different price, or a different combination of products? Price-volume-mix (PVM) analysis splits the total variance into those effects, and the pieces must add up exactly to the total. If they do not, the analysis will not survive the first question from the CFO.

Price variance = (actual price − budget price) × actual quantity, product by product. Volume variance = (actual total quantity − budget total quantity) × budget average price: what the extra units would have brought at the budget mix. Mix variance = for each product, (actual quantity − actual total quantity × budget share) × budget price: the effect of selling relatively more of cheaper or more expensive products. Volume and mix together equal the sum of (actual quantity − budget quantity) × budget price.

In the example, the budget is 600 units of A at 100 and 400 units of B at 150, so 120,000 of revenue at an average price of 120. The actual is 770 A at 98 and 330 B at 155, so 126,610. Price: (98 − 100) × 770 + (155 − 150) × 330 = −1,540 + 1,650 = +110. Volume: 100 extra units × 120 = +12,000. Mix: at the budget mix, 1,100 units would be 660 A and 440 B; we sold 110 more A at 100 and 110 fewer B at 150, so 11,000 − 16,500 = −5,500. Check: 110 + 12,000 − 5,500 = 6,610 = 126,610 − 120,000.

The story is in the pieces: total revenue is up 6,610, but the shift to product A cost 5,500. If B carries the better margin, the margin analysis looks worse than the revenue one, which is why many teams run PVM on contribution margin (using budget margin per unit instead of budget price) rather than on revenue. Name the method on the slide: the order of the calculation (price at actual or budget quantity) changes how the pieces are split, never the total.
points: Price variance = (actual price − budget price) × actual quantity.
Volume variance = (actual total units − budget total units) × budget average price.
Mix variance = (actual units − actual total × budget share) × budget price, per product.
Price + volume + mix must equal the total variance exactly.
Run PVM on margin when products have different margins; state the method.

example.note: Budget mix: 60 % A, 40 % B, so 1,100 units at budget mix = 660 A and 440 B.

lessons.title: Costs: fixed and variable, cost centres, allocations, break-even
text: A variable cost moves with volume (raw materials, packaging, delivery per order, sales commissions); a fixed cost does not move in the short term (rent, salaried staff, insurance, straight-line depreciation). Many costs are semi-variable, such as a phone contract with a fixed fee plus usage, or step costs, such as one more supervisor every 20 operators. The split decides how costs are flexed in the budget and how profit reacts when volume changes.

Contribution margin = revenue − variable costs. Per unit, with a price of 80 and a variable cost of 50, each unit contributes 30 towards fixed costs, a contribution margin ratio of 37.5 %. Break-even (point mort, seuil de rentabilité) is the volume where contribution covers fixed costs: 240,000 / 30 = 8,000 units, or 640,000 of revenue. At 10,000 units, profit is 10,000 × 30 − 240,000 = 60,000, and the margin of safety is (800,000 − 640,000) / 800,000 = 20 %: sales can fall 20 % before the company loses money.

Costs are tracked by cost centre: a department or team with a manager responsible for its spending (IT, HR, a warehouse). Profit centres are responsible for revenue and costs (a business unit), investment centres for capital as well. Each manager gets a report of the lines they control, which is why the chart of cost centres must match the real organisation.

Shared costs such as IT, HR or head office are often allocated to the business units with an allocation key (clé de répartition): headcount, square metres, revenue, number of tickets. 90,000 of IT cost allocated by headcount between Sales (30 people), Operations (50) and Admin (20) gives 27,000, 45,000 and 18,000. Choose keys that reflect what drives the cost, explain them, and keep them stable, or managers will spend the reviews arguing about allocations they cannot control. Activity-based costing (ABC) refines this by allocating through activities (orders processed, deliveries) instead of one key.

Two classic traps: deciding on a product using fully allocated cost (dropping a product with a positive contribution but a negative allocated result makes the company poorer, because the fixed costs stay), and calling a cost fixed when it is only fixed within a range of volume.
points: Variable costs move with volume, fixed costs do not in the short term; watch semi-variable and step costs.
Contribution margin = revenue − variable costs; break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit.
Margin of safety = (sales − break-even sales) / sales.
Cost centre (costs), profit centre (revenue and costs), investment centre (also capital).
Allocation keys should follow the cost driver, be explained and stay stable.

example.code:
Fixed costs                 240,000
Price per unit                   80
Variable cost per unit           50
Contribution margin per unit     30   (80 - 50)
Contribution margin ratio     37.5%   (30 / 80)
Break-even                    8,000 units   (240,000 / 30)
                            640,000 revenue (240,000 / 37.5%)
At 10,000 units: profit = 10,000 x 30 - 240,000 = 60,000
Margin of safety = (800,000 - 640,000) / 800,000 = 20%

lessons.title: Month-end close and the management reporting pack
text: Every month, accounting closes the books: invoices, accruals for costs received but not yet invoiced, prepayments, depreciation, payroll, intercompany entries. Good groups close in 3 to 5 working days (WD3 to WD5). FP&A starts before the close is final: it reviews the preliminary numbers on WD2-WD3, chases unusual entries with accounting, then prepares the pack and the commentary for the management meeting around WD5-WD8.

The management reporting pack usually holds: a one-page summary with the key messages, the P&L by business unit against budget, last forecast and last year, the KPIs (orders, backlog, headcount, gross margin %, DSO for receivables, cash), an EBITDA bridge from budget to actual, the variance commentary and the updated full-year outlook. Start with the message, not the tables: managers read the first page and the bridge.

A bridge (or waterfall) chart walks from one number to another through its causes: budget EBITDA 80,000, volume +12,000, price −4,000, cost of sales rate −6,000, opex savings +6,000, actual EBITDA 88,000. Each bar is one cause, the bars add up exactly, and the order follows the story. Excel has a built-in waterfall chart and Power BI a waterfall visual.

Know your definitions. EBITDA is not defined by IFRS or US GAAP: it is a non-GAAP measure, or an alternative performance measure in Europe, and the company sets its definition. Since IFRS 16 (2019), most leases are on the balance sheet and rent is replaced by depreciation and interest, which raises EBITDA; under US GAAP (ASC 842), operating lease cost stays in operating expenses. A pack that compares years across that change without saying so misleads its readers.

Tools: Excel is everywhere (models, reconciliations, quick analysis); Power BI or Tableau for the dashboards and the drill-down; EPM tools (enterprise performance management) such as Anaplan, Oracle EPM (formerly Hyperion), Workday Adaptive Planning, SAP Analytics Cloud, Board, Pigment or CCH Tagetik hold the budget and forecast versions, the workflow and the consolidation, so that the model is not 40 linked spreadsheets. The ERP (SAP, Oracle, Sage, Microsoft Dynamics) is the source of the actuals.
points: Close in 3-5 working days; FP&A reviews the preliminary numbers before the final close.
The pack: summary, P&L by business unit vs budget / forecast / last year, KPIs, bridge, commentary, outlook.
A bridge (waterfall) walks from budget to actual by cause; the bars add up exactly.
EBITDA is a non-GAAP measure; IFRS 16 moved most rent out of EBITDA, US GAAP operating leases did not.
Excel for models, Power BI for dashboards, EPM tools (Anaplan, Oracle EPM, Adaptive) for planning, the ERP for actuals.

example.code:
EBITDA bridge, budget to actual (month)
Budget EBITDA                 80,000
  Volume                     +12,000
  Price                       -4,000
  Cost of sales rate          -6,000
  Opex savings                +6,000
Actual EBITDA                 88,000
example.note: Same month as the budget vs actual table of lesson 4: volume, price and cost of sales explain the +2,000 of gross margin.

lessons.title: Business partnering: presenting, challenging, scenarios
text: A business partner is the finance person a manager calls before deciding, not after. That means knowing the business drivers as well as the numbers, being on time with the reporting, and turning analysis into a recommendation: "we should delay the second hire to Q3; it keeps the department on budget and the backlog does not need it before then".

Presenting to managers: one message per slide, the conclusion first, the numbers that support it next, the detail in the appendix. Use their words (orders, clients, projects) rather than account numbers, round the figures (520k, not 519,873.42) and always give the comparison (against budget, forecast or last year). Prepare the three questions you will be asked and the numbers that answer them.

Challenging a budget or a forecast is part of the job, and it is about evidence, not opinion. Compare the plan with history (a 25 % growth after three years at 5 %), with the pipeline (signed contracts, conversion rates), with capacity (can the team deliver it, are the hires planned?) and with the market. Ask what has to be true for the number to happen. When a manager pushes back, look at their drivers together, agree what changes, and record the assumption with its owner.

Scenario planning prepares the decisions before the surprise: a base case, a downside and an upside, each built from a few explicit drivers (volume, price, cost inflation), with the actions planned for each one (freeze hiring at a given revenue level, for example). Sensitivity analysis changes one driver at a time to show which ones matter most. Present the range, not just the base case: "EBITDA between 108k and 233k, 180k in the base case" is more honest and more useful than one number.
points: Business partner = the finance person consulted before the decision.
Conclusion first, comparison always, rounded numbers, detail in the appendix.
Challenge with evidence: history, pipeline, capacity, market; ask what has to be true.
Scenarios: base, downside, upside from explicit drivers, with planned actions; sensitivity changes one driver at a time.
Record every assumption with its owner.

example.code:
Scenario   Volume  Price   Units   Price   Revenue    EBITDA
Downside    -10%    -2%    9,000   117.6  1,058,400   108,400
Base          0%     0%   10,000   120.0  1,200,000   180,000
Upside       +8%    +1%   10,800   121.2  1,308,960   232,960
Variable cost 70 per unit, fixed costs 320,000
EBITDA = units x (price - 70) - 320,000
example.note: Owners of the assumptions: Sales (volume), Pricing (price), Operations (costs).

Summary, P&L by business unit, KPIs, bridge, commentary, outlook

pitfalls: Reporting a variance without saying whether it is favourable or unfavourable, or mixing sign conventions between revenue and cost lines.
Price, volume and mix effects that do not add up to the total variance.
Commentary that repeats the table ("costs were higher than budget") instead of giving the cause, the amount and the impact on the forecast.
Blaming managers for variances caused by FX rates, scope changes or volume: restate at constant currency and flex the budget.
Dropping a product with a positive contribution margin because its fully allocated result is negative: the fixed costs stay.
Overwriting the approved budget with forecast updates: the year then has no fixed reference.
A forecast built by extending the run-rate, ignoring seasonality and signed contracts.

exercises.q: In E2, the revenue variance % (variance compared with the budget).
exercises.hint: Variance % = (actual − budget) / budget. Use the cells, not the typed numbers.
exercises.explain: (504000 − 480000) / 480000 = 0.05, so +5 %. Using D2/B2 gives the same result. If a budget can be negative or zero (a loss line, a new product), divide by ABS(B2) and wrap the formula in IFERROR, or the sign and the error will mislead the reader.

exercises.q: In E3, write Favourable if the travel cost (a cost line) is at or below budget, otherwise Unfavourable.
exercises.hint: For a cost, spending less than or exactly the budget is good news: IF(actual <= budget, …, …).
exercises.explain: 21600 is above the 18000 budget, so Unfavourable. For a revenue line the test is the other way round (actual >= budget). In a real report, a single formula can handle both with the Type column: IF(B3="Cost", IF(D3<=C3, …), IF(D3>=C3, …)).

exercises.q: In F2, the volume variance in revenue: the extra units valued at the budget price.
exercises.hint: Volume variance = (actual units − budget units) × budget price.
exercises.explain: (1100 − 1000) × 50 = +5000, favourable. The price variance would be (48 − 50) × 1100 = −2200, and the two add up to the total revenue variance: 1100 × 48 − 1000 × 50 = 52800 − 50000 = 2800 = 5000 − 2200.

exercises.q: In D2, the break-even volume in units.
exercises.hint: Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit (price − variable cost).
exercises.explain: 240000 / (80 − 50) = 8000 units. Each unit contributes 30 towards the fixed costs. The brackets matter: A2/B2-C2 divides first and gives 2950. In revenue, the break-even is 8000 × 80 = 640000, or A2/((B2-C2)/B2).

exercises.q: In D2, a full-year run-rate forecast: the actuals from January to June plus the average of the last three months for each of the six remaining months.
exercises.hint: Year to date = SUM of the six months; the run-rate = AVERAGE of April to June × 6 months left.
exercises.explain: 2586 + 451 × 6 = 5292 (thousand euros). The last three months are used because they reflect the current pace better than the whole half-year. It is a sanity check: a real forecast also adds the seasonality of the second half, signed contracts and planned price changes.

exercises.q: Put the steps of an annual budget cycle in order.
steps: Finance sends the guidelines and top-down targets
Departments build their budgets from their drivers
Finance consolidates and challenges the gaps to target
The approved budget is locked in the reporting tool and monthly tracking starts
exercises.answer: Guidelines first so everyone uses the same assumptions, then the bottom-up build, consolidation and challenge, iterations, approval, and finally the locked version that every month is compared with.

exercises.q: Sort these costs of a company that makes and delivers furniture into fixed and variable costs (short term).
exercises.answer: Variable costs move with the number of pieces sold; fixed costs stay the same at 1,000 or 1,500 pieces a month. Some are step costs in reality: a second factory or a new shift would change the fixed costs.

exercises.q: Match each term with its definition.
pairs: Change in total units valued at the budget average price
Effect of selling a different combination of products
Always looks the same number of months ahead
Cost budget restated at the actual volume
exercises.answer: Price, volume and mix explain a revenue or margin variance and add up to it; the rolling forecast and the flexed budget are ways to compare with something relevant.

exercises.q: A product sells at 80 with a variable cost of 50. What is its contribution margin ratio, in percent?
exercises.answer: (80 − 50) / 80 = 30 / 80 = 0.375, so 37.5 %. Each euro of revenue leaves 37.5 cents to cover fixed costs; with 240,000 of fixed costs, break-even revenue is 240,000 / 0.375 = 640,000.

exercises.q: Marketing spent 52,500 against a budget of 60,000 at the end of June. The manager says the campaigns moved to September. How do you report it?
options: A favourable variance of 7,500: a saving to celebrate
A favourable variance of 7,500 explained as timing: the spending is expected in September and the full-year forecast does not change
An unfavourable variance, because the plan was not followed
No variance: it will even out by year end
exercises.answer: The variance is real and favourable at the end of June, but it is a timing difference, not a saving. Saying so prevents the money from being counted twice (once as a saving, once spent in September) and keeps the full-year forecast honest.

exercises.q: The sales director of a region forecasts +25 % revenue next year. The region grew 4 to 6 % a year for three years.

steps.text: In the forecast meeting, what do you do first?

choices.label: Ask what drives the +25 %: new clients, prices, products, and how much is already signed
choices.feedback: Start from the drivers. A big number can be right, but it needs evidence the business owns.

choices.label: Cut it to +6 % in your model, in line with history
choices.feedback: Overriding the manager without discussion loses their trust and their ownership of the number.

choices.label: Accept it: the sales director knows the market better
choices.feedback: Finance is expected to challenge. An unchallenged optimistic forecast becomes the variance you will explain all year.

steps.text: The director shows a pipeline: 3 large deals worth 18 points of growth, none signed yet. What next?

choices.label: Weight the deals by their probability in the base case and show the full +25 % as an upside scenario
choices.feedback: The base case stays credible, the upside is visible, and each deal is an assumption with an owner.

choices.label: Keep +25 % because the deals exist
choices.feedback: Unsigned deals at 100 % is how forecasts become optimistic every year.

choices.label: Remove the deals from the forecast entirely
choices.feedback: Zero probability is as wrong as 100 %: some deals in a pipeline do close.

steps.text: How do you record the agreement?

choices.label: Write the assumptions (deals, probabilities, prices) with the director as owner, and track them each month
choices.feedback: When the actual comes in, you will know which assumption was wrong, and the next forecast improves.

choices.label: Just keep the final number in the forecast file
choices.feedback: Without the assumptions, nobody can explain the variance in six months.

exercises.answer: Challenge with evidence and drivers, weight what is not signed, show the range with scenarios, and record each assumption with its owner.

exercises.q: Write the variance commentary for this month: revenue 520k vs a 500k budget, cost of sales 318k vs 300k, opex 114k vs 120k, EBITDA 88k vs 80k. You know that volume brought +12k EBITDA, prices −4k (discount for a key client, continuing all year), the cost of sales rate −6k (freight prices up, expected to last two more months) and opex +6k (two hires delayed from May to July).
exercises.answer: EBITDA 88k, +8k (+10 %) vs budget, favourable. Revenue +20k (+4 %), mainly volume: higher volumes added +12k of EBITDA, partly offset by −4k of price from the discount granted to a key client, which continues for the rest of the year (about −4k a month in the forecast). Gross margin +2k only, because freight prices raised the cost of sales rate (−6k); we expect this for two more months. Opex −6k vs budget (favourable) is timing: two hires moved from May to July, so the saving reverses from July. Full-year outlook: the forecast now includes the discount for the rest of the year (about −4k a month) and freight for two more months (about −6k a month); the opex saving is not a saving and stays out of the outlook. The forecast is updated at the next re-forecast.

interview.q: What is the difference between a budget and a forecast?
interview.a: The budget is the plan approved before the year starts; it sets targets and stays fixed so performance can be measured against it. The forecast is the updated view of where the year will land, revised quarterly (3+9, 6+6, 9+3) or continuously with a rolling forecast. Variances are usually shown against both: the budget says whether we met our commitment, the forecast whether we are where we said we would be last time.

interview.q: Revenue is above budget but EBITDA is below. How would you investigate?
interview.a: I would build a bridge from budget to actual EBITDA. On revenue I would split price, volume and mix: higher volume of low-margin products can raise revenue and lower margin. Then the cost of sales rate (purchase prices, freight, FX on purchases), then opex by cost centre, checking for one-offs, accruals and timing. I would also check FX and scope effects. The answer is a short list of causes with amounts that add up to the EBITDA variance.

interview.q: Walk me through a price, volume and mix analysis.
interview.a: Price variance is the price difference times the actual quantity, product by product. Volume is the change in total units times the budget average price or margin. Mix is the difference between the actual units and the actual total at the budget mix, times the budget price or margin. The three add up exactly to the total variance. I prefer to do it on contribution margin, because a mix shift to cheaper products can hurt margin more than revenue, and I state the method because the order of calculation changes the split.

interview.q: How do you build a forecast for a business you do not know yet?
interview.a: Start with the history: monthly actuals for two or three years to see trend and seasonality. Then agree a few drivers with the business: customers, orders, average price, headcount, and who owns each assumption. Build the model from those drivers, cross-check it against a simple run-rate and the pipeline, and present a base case with an upside and a downside. Then measure accuracy every month and fix the drivers that are biased.

interview.q: A manager disagrees with your numbers in a meeting. What do you do?
interview.a: Listen to the specific point first: is it the data, an allocation or an assumption? If it is a data error, I check it right after the meeting and correct it openly. If it is an assumption, I show the driver and the evidence, ask what they know that I do not, and agree a version with a named owner. I avoid arguing totals in front of everyone; the aim is a number we both understand and can defend.

interview.q: What is break-even and how do you use it?
interview.a: Break-even is the volume where the contribution margin covers fixed costs: fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. With fixed costs of 240k, a price of 80 and a variable cost of 50, it is 8,000 units, 640k of revenue. I use it for pricing and launch decisions and to compute the margin of safety, which tells how far sales can fall before the business loses money. It depends on a clean split between fixed and variable costs, which is usually the hard part.

interview.q: Which tools have you used for planning and reporting?
interview.a: Excel for models and reconciliations, with structured sheets, inputs separated from formulas and checks that totals tie to the ledger. Power BI for the reporting pack and drill-down, connected to the ERP data rather than pasted values. I know how EPM tools such as Anaplan, Oracle EPM or Workday Adaptive Planning manage versions, workflow and driver-based models, and I can learn the one the company uses; the logic of the model matters more than the tool.

interview.q: Why do allocations cause arguments, and how do you handle them?
interview.a: Managers are judged on numbers that include costs they do not control. I choose keys that follow what drives the cost (headcount for HR, tickets for IT support), explain them in the budget guidelines and keep them stable during the year. In the reporting I show contribution before allocations next to the result after allocations, so a manager is judged on what they control, and decisions such as dropping a product are taken on contribution, not on allocated results.
